content: Niaprazine, also known by the brand name Nopron, is a sedative-hypnotic medication that belongs to the phenylpiperazine class of drugs. It has been utilized for the treatment of sleep disturbances since the early 1970s in various European countries, including France, Italy, and Luxembourg. This drug is particularly favored for use in children and adolescents due to its excellent safety and tolerability profile, as well as its lack of potential for abuse. Initially, niaprazine was thought to function as an antihistamine and anticholinergic agent. However, subsequent research revealed that it does not exhibit significant binding affinity for either histamine H1 receptors or muscarinic acetylcholine (mACh) receptors, with binding affinity values (Ki) exceeding 1 μM. Instead, niaprazine was found to act as a potent and selective antagonist of the 5-HT2A serotonin receptor and the α1-adrenergic receptor, with binding affinity values of 75 nM and 86 nM, respectively. Niaprazine demonstrates negligible activity at several other receptor sites, including 5-HT1A, 5-HT2B, dopamine D2, and β-adrenergic receptors, as well as at the serotonin transporter (SERT) and vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT), with binding affinity values exceeding 1 μM for all of these targets. However, it does exhibit weak binding affinity for the α2-adrenergic receptor, with a Ki value of 730 nM, where it likely acts as an antagonist. The metabolism of niaprazine results in the production of a compound known as para-fluorophenylpiperazine (pFPP), in a manner similar to how the drugs trazodone and nefazodone are metabolized into meta-chlorophenylpiperazine (mCPP). The role of pFPP in the clinical effects of niaprazine remains unclear. However, animal studies have shown that, unlike niaprazine, pFPP does not produce sedative effects. Instead, pFPP appears to exhibit a behavioral profile consistent with serotonergic activation.
